title: The eight who receive
hook: the Qur'an names who zakat is for: the poor, the needy, debtors, travelers and others (9:60)

segments.voice: Yesterday: shahada, and a clean page for anyone new. Your line was everyone started new. Today, the verse that gives zakat its addresses, one of them for hearts being drawn close. Day one hundred fifty-two.

You've worked out the number: two and a half percent, ready to go. Now what? Hand it to the first person who asks? Drop it in any collection box? Give it to your cousin who's always broke? Most giving is left to the giver's judgment. Zakat is unusual. The Qur'an doesn't just say give. It gives you the list. One verse, in Surah at-Tawbah, names exactly who zakat is for. Eight kinds of people. Eight addresses.
screen: `THE NUMBER IS READY. NOW WHAT?` → `NOT JUST GIVE: HERE'S THE LIST.` → `EIGHT ADDRESSES.`

segments.voice: Chapter nine, verse sixty. In Pickthall's translation it begins: The alms are only for the poor and the needy. Here are all eight. One, the poor, al-fuqara'. Two, the needy, al-masakin. Scholars differ on which of the two is worse off, but together they're the people who can't cover the basics. Three, the workers who collect and manage zakat, paid from it so the system runs. Four, those whose hearts are to be reconciled: people new to Islam, or whose goodwill the community needs. Five, to free the captives. In the Prophet's time that meant helping enslaved people buy their freedom; some scholars today apply it to freeing people from captivity and trafficking. Six, the debtors, crushed by debts taken on for a decent reason. Seven, in the cause of Allah. Classically this meant those fighting in defense of the community; some modern scholars read it more widely, for example for education and dawah, and others keep it narrow. Eight, the wayfarer, stranded far from home, even if rich back there. The verse ends: a duty from Allah. Notice what the list doesn't name: the mosque's new carpet, or the giver's own family. The jurists say zakat isn't paid to your own parents or children, because you already owe them support. Bukhari reports that when the Prophet ﷺ sent Mu'adh to Yemen, he told him to take it from their rich and return it to their poor. Local, specific, human. Zakat doesn't vanish into a fog called charity. It has addresses.
screen: `9:60 — THE POOR AND THE NEEDY.` · `WORKERS, HEARTS, CAPTIVES.` · `DEBTORS, THE CAUSE, THE TRAVELER.` · `FROM THEIR RICH TO THEIR POOR.` · then, large: `IT HAS ADDRESSES.`

segments.voice: Count the eight on your fingers, slowly, and give each a real face: the poor, the needy, the one who collects, a heart being welcomed, a captive, someone drowning in debt, the cause of Allah, a traveler stranded at a station at midnight. Go through them twice, and notice which face stays with you longest.
Zakat, given to the eight kinds of people Surah at-Tawbah names: the poor, the needy, the workers, reconciled hearts, captives, debtors, the cause of Allah, and the traveler.
Your line: it has addresses. Eight fingers, eight faces, eight kinds of people. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims direct their zakat to the eight categories named in 9:60, often through mosques or zakat organizations, preferring local recipients, and not to their own parents or children.

chat.says: Can I give my zakat to anyone I like, even my own kids?
options: Zakat has eight named kinds of receivers, and not your own parents or children.
Yes, anyone in need counts, including your kids if they're short this month.
Any good cause works; the Qur'an leaves zakat to the giver's judgment.
